main.title: Artificial intelligence: the Dartmouth workshop
main.subtitle: A field takes its name
main.summary: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was a 1956 summer workshop widely considered to be the founding event of artificial intelligence as a field.

cards.heading: A field takes its name
cards.text:
The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was a 1956 summer workshop widely considered to be the founding event of artificial intelligence as a field. The workshop has been referred to as "the Constitutional Convention of AI". The project's four organizers, Claude Shannon, John McCarthy, Nathaniel Rochester and Marvin Minsky, are considered some of the "founding fathers" of AI. The workshop followed earlier discussions at the 1951 Paris cybernetics conference and the Macy meetings.

The project lasted approximately six to eight weeks and consisted largely of brainstorming sessions. Eleven mathematicians and scientists originally planned to attend; not all of them attended, but more than ten others came for short times.

main.title: IBM 305 RAMAC
main.summary: The IBM 305 RAMAC was the first commercial computer that used a moving-head hard disk drive (magnetic disk storage) for secondary storage.

cards.heading: IBM 305 RAMAC
cards.text: The IBM 305 RAMAC was the first commercial computer that used a moving-head hard disk drive (magnetic disk storage) for secondary storage. The system was publicly announced on September 14, 1956, with test units already installed at the U.S. Navy and at private corporations. RAMAC stood for "Random Access Method of Accounting and Control", as its design was motivated by the need for real-time accounting in business.

main.title: Fairchild Semiconductor
main.summary: Founded in 1957 by engineers leaving Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory, Fairchild became a pioneer in transistors and integrated circuits.

cards.heading: Fairchild Semiconductor
cards.text:
Fairchild Semiconductor International, Inc. was an American semiconductor company based in San Jose, California. It was founded in 1957 as a division of Fairchild Camera and Instrument by the "traitorous eight" who defected from Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory. It became a pioneer in the manufacturing of transistors and of integrated circuits. Schlumberger bought the firm in 1979 and sold it to National Semiconductor in 1987; Fairchild was spun off as an independent company again in 1997. In September 2016, Fairchild was acquired by ON Semiconductor.

The company had locations in the United States in San Jose, California; San Rafael, California; South Portland, Maine; West Jordan, Utah; Puyallup, Washington; and Mountaintop, Pennsylvania. Outside the US, it operated locations in Australia; Singapore; Bucheon, South Korea; Penang, Malaysia; Suzhou, China; and Cebu City, Philippines, among others.

main.title: IBM delivers the first Fortran compiler
main.summary: IBM delivered its first Fortran compiler in April 1957, following a reference manual issued the previous year.

cards.heading: IBM delivers the first Fortran compiler
cards.text: IBM delivered its first Fortran compiler in April 1957, following a reference manual issued the previous year. The language made numerical and scientific programs easier to write, giving engineers and researchers a tool suited to calculation. Its applications grew to include weather prediction, fluid dynamics, physics and chemistry, as well as high-performance computing. Later versions added structured programming, arrays, modules and parallel operations. A 1966 American standard helped limit differences between compilers, supporting the language's continued use across successive generations of computers.

main.title: Sputnik 1
main.summary: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957, placing the first artificial satellite in Earth orbit.

cards.heading: Sputnik 1
cards.text: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957, placing the first artificial satellite in Earth orbit. Its polished metal sphere measured 58 centimetres across, with four antennas transmitting radio pulses that amateurs could detect. The signal continued for three weeks until its batteries ran out. Atmospheric drag brought the satellite down on 4 January 1958. Its success surprised the United States and helped trigger the Space Race, turning a small orbiting transmitter into an event with political, military and scientific consequences.

main.title: Kilby demonstrates the integrated circuit
main.summary: Jack Kilby demonstrated an integrated circuit in 1958, showing how electronic components could be combined in a compact device.

cards.heading: Kilby demonstrates the integrated circuit
cards.text: Jack Kilby demonstrated an integrated circuit in 1958, showing how electronic components could be combined in a compact device. Bringing components and connections together reduced the space required by assemblies of separate parts. Integrated circuits developed into chips containing transistors, resistors and capacitors on semiconductor material, commonly silicon. Mass production and standardised designs helped lower costs while increasing reliability and complexity. The approach enabled smaller equipment and became central to computing, memory, control and power management across modern electronic devices.

main.title: Vertigo
main.summary: Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo appeared in 1958, following a former San Francisco detective hired to investigate an acquaintance's wife.

cards.heading: Vertigo
cards.text: Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo appeared in 1958, following a former San Francisco detective hired to investigate an acquaintance's wife. James Stewart plays the investigator, whose fear of heights and vertigo complicate his work; Kim Novak plays the woman he follows. The film adapted Boileau-Narcejac's novel From Among the Dead and used San Francisco locations alongside studio filming. Its dolly zoom distorted perspective to convey the detective's disorientation. The effect became so closely associated with the film that it is often called the Vertigo effect.

main.title: COBOL
main.summary: COBOL's design began in 1959 as part of an American effort to create a portable language for business data processing.

cards.heading: COBOL
cards.text: COBOL's design began in 1959 as part of an American effort to create a portable language for business data processing. CODASYL drew partly on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC, using English-like instructions to express business operations. Department of Defense pressure encouraged computer manufacturers to support it, helping adoption spread. Standardised in 1968, COBOL became deeply embedded in finance, administration and large-scale transaction processing. Its long service meant later work often involved maintaining established applications or moving them to new systems, extending the life of an initially temporary solution.

main.title: MOSFET
main.summary: In electronics, the metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET, MOS-FET, MOS FET, or MOS transistor) is a type of field-effect transistor (FET), most commonly fabricated by the controlled oxidation of silicon.

cards.heading: MOSFET
cards.text:
In electronics, the metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET, MOS-FET, MOS FET, or MOS transistor) is a type of field-effect transistor (FET), most commonly fabricated by the controlled oxidation of silicon. It has an insulated gate, the voltage of which determines the conductivity of the device. This ability to change conductivity with the amount of applied voltage can be used for amplifying or switching electronic signals. The term metal–insulator–semiconductor field-effect transistor (MISFET) is almost synonymous with MOSFET. Another near-synonym is insulated-gate field-effect transistor (IGFET).

Physicist Julius Edgar Lilienfeld first proposed the concept of a field-effect transistor (FET) in 1925, but it was not possible to construct a working device at that time. The first working metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) was invented in 1959 by engineers Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs. Their breakthrough—fabricating a practical field-effect transistor enabled by Atalla’s earlier work on silicon surface passivation and thermal oxidation—revolutionized electronics and paved the way for smaller and cheaper radios, calculators, computers, and other electronic devices.

main.title: The Twilight Zone
main.summary: The Twilight Zone began on CBS on 2 October 1959, with Rod Serling presenting self-contained stories of disturbing and unusual events.

cards.heading: The Twilight Zone
cards.text: The Twilight Zone began on CBS on 2 October 1959, with Rod Serling presenting self-contained stories of disturbing and unusual events. Each episode placed ordinary characters in an unfamiliar situation, often ending with a surprise and a moral. Serling's opening and closing narration framed these journeys; as head writer, he wrote or co-wrote 92 of the 156 episodes. The series ran for five seasons until 1964. Its title entered everyday speech as a way to describe a surreal experience beyond familiar expectations.
